idiom_name: initialisation in main/val members (objects and lazy vals are the lazy alternative); Futures start on creation
implementation_notes: Scala's default is the opposite of eager: an object is created lazily when it is first referenced, exactly like a lazy val, so the eager form must be deliberate - initialise in main (@main or a class whose val members acquire at construction) or force the objects you depend on during start-up instead of letting the first request trigger them. Futures are the eager exception inside the language: Future { ... } hands the computation to the ExecutionContext when it is created, so creating the warm-up futures is the acquisition and readiness is Await/Future.sequence on their completion rather than a check that they exist; effect types such as IO and ZIO are descriptions and stay lazy until run, which is the same eager-versus-lazy fork one level up.
pitfalls: Class and object initialisation failures are wrapped by the JVM as ExceptionInInitializerError and the class stays unusable, so retryable acquisition belongs in a method rather than in a val.
Eagerly started Futures on the global ExecutionContext keep running and their failures stay silent unless the future is observed, so an unawaited warm-up wastes work and hides breakage.
Trait initialisation order (linearisation) combined with eager vals is a classic source of nulls during construction; inject dependencies instead of reading eagerly initialised members.
